If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Every invertible matrix $A\in M_n(\mathbb F)$, where $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, has a unique factorisation

$$A=QR,$$

where $Q^*Q=I$ and $R$ is upper triangular with positive real diagonal entries. Thus $Q$ is orthogonal over $\mathbb R$ and unitary over $\mathbb C$. The assertion includes the unique $0\times0$ factorisation.

derivations.claim: A basis of the orthogonal complement completes the columns of X to an invertible square matrix.
Square QR of the completion yields the rectangular factorization and orthonormal completion.
The triangular factor identities give the projection formula P_X=QQ^T.

boundaries.reason: The hypotheses require n>p>=1, so the zero-dimensional design case is excluded.
Full column rank with p>=1 excludes a zero-column design and makes R invertible.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement includes p=1 and step 2.1 applies square QR to the invertible completion.

The factorization has no interval or parameter endpoint case.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $n>p\ge1$ and let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ have full column rank. Then there are matrices $Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ and $R\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ such that

$$X=QR,$$

where $Q^TQ=I_p$ and $R$ is upper triangular with positive diagonal. The columns of $Q$ can be completed to an orthonormal basis $[Q\ Q_0]$ of $\mathbb R^n$, with $Q_0\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-p)}$. For $P_X:=X(X^TX)^{-1}X^T$, one has $P_X=QQ^T$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z\sim N_n(0,I_n)$ have independent standard-normal coordinates, and let $U\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ satisfy $U^TU=I_n$. Then $UZ$ also has independent $N(0,1)$ coordinates. Here $I_n$ is the identity matrix and $U$ is orthogonal.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For an integer $k\ge1$, let $G=(G_1,\ldots,G_k)$ have law $N_k(0,I_k)$, so its coordinates are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables. The **chi-square law with $k$ degrees of freedom**, denoted $\chi_k^2$, is the law of
$$
Q_k=\sum_{j=1}^k G_j^2=\|G\|^2.
$$
For $k=0$, define $\chi_0^2=\delta_0$, the point mass at zero. This zero-degree law records a rank-zero projection only; it is not used as a denominator in a Student or Fisher ratio. The multivariate-normal characteristic-function theorem makes the definition independent of the chosen realization of $G$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every integer $k\ge1$, the law $\chi_k^2$ has density
$$
f_k(x)=c_k x^{k/2-1}e^{-x/2}\mathbf 1_{\{x>0\}},\qquad c_k=\frac{\sigma_{k-1}(S^{k-1})}{2(2\pi)^{k/2}}>0,
$$
where $\sigma_{k-1}$ is the polar surface measure on the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^k$. Consequently, $Q_k>0$ almost surely, and its cumulative distribution function is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a positive integer $k$, take the product probability law of an independent standard normal $G$ and an independent $Q_k\sim\chi_k^2$. The **Student t law with $k$ degrees of freedom**, denoted $t_k$, is the law of
$$T_k=\begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{G}{\sqrt{Q_k/k}},&Q_k>0,\\ 0,&Q_k\le0. \end{cases}$$
For positive integers $r,s$, take independent $Q_r\sim\chi_r^2$ and $Q_s\sim\chi_s^2$. The **Fisher F law with degrees $(r,s)$**, denoted $F_{r,s}$, is the law of
$$F_{r,s}=\begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{Q_r/r}{Q_s/s},&Q_s>0,\\ 0,&Q_s\le0. \end{cases}$$
The displayed piecewise maps are defined on all of $\mathbb R^2$ and are Borel measurable: each quotient is continuous on its Borel positive-denominator region, and the value on the complementary Borel nonpositive-denominator region is constant. The positive-degree chi-square lemma proves that the denominators are positive almost surely, so these versions agree almost surely with the usual quotients. Zero degrees are excluded from both definitions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every $k\ge1$, the CDF of $t_k$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$, is symmetric about zero, and has limits $0$ and $1$ at $-\infty$ and $+\infty$. For every $r,s\ge1$, the CDF of $F_{r,s}$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$, is zero on $(-\infty,0]$, and is strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$ with limit $1$ at $+\infty$. Consequently, for each $u\in(0,1)$ each law has exactly one $u$-quantile on its support.

A **randomized test** is a randomized procedure with binary action space
whose action set is $\{0,1\}$, equipped with its full sigma-algebra
$2^{\{0,1\}}$ (the power set, which is a sigma-algebra by
[[def-sigma-algebra]]), where $1$ means reject and $0$ means do not reject
([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its **test function** is
$$\varphi(x)=K(x,\{1\}),\qquad x\in\mathcal X.$$
Since $K(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure and $\{0\},\{1\}$ partition the
action set, $K(x,\{0\})+K(x,\{1\})=1$. Thus $\varphi(x)\in[0,1]$ and
$1-\varphi(x)=K(x,\{0\})$ is the probability of not rejecting. Give $[0,1]$
the trace of the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,+\infty]$, namely
$\{C\cap[0,1]:C\in\mathcal B([0,+\infty])\}$. By
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], $x\mapsto K(x,\{1\})$ is
measurable; since it has range in $[0,1]$, its preimage of $C\cap[0,1]$ equals
its preimage of $C$ and is measurable for every such $C$. Hence $\varphi$ is a
measurable map in the preimage sense of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Its value is the
rejection probability after observing $x$.
The convention $1=\text{reject}$ is fixed here. No null or alternative
hypothesis is part of this definition.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Let
$\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ be nonempty disjoint subsets of $\Theta$, called the null
and alternative hypotheses. A hypothesis is **simple** when it is a singleton
and **composite** when it has at least two elements.

For a randomized test with test function
$\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ ([[def-randomized-test]]), its **power function**
is
$$\beta(\theta):=E_\theta[\varphi(X)]\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
Its **size** is
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\beta(\theta),$$
and it has **level $\alpha$** when this supremum is at most
$\alpha\in[0,1]$. The expectations exist and lie in $[0,1]$ because
$0\le\varphi\le1$ and each $P_\theta$ is a probability measure
([[def-probability-measure]],
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).
The supremum exists because $\Theta_0$ is nonempty, the values lie in
$[0,1]$, and $\mathbb R$ has the least-upper-bound property
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

For the binary action $a\in\{0,1\}$, where $1$ means reject, the
**zero-one error loss** is $1$ when $a=1$ and $\theta\in\Theta_0$, or when
$a=0$ and $\theta\in\Theta_1$, and is $0$ otherwise. The decision-rule risk
from [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] integrates this loss against the action
kernel and data law. For each fixed $\theta$, its section on the binary
action space is measurable. The risk identities proved in
[[lem-test-zero-one-loss-risk-identities]] show that risk equals
$\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_0$ and $1-\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_1$. Thus size
is the worst null error risk, and power is the rejection probability under
each alternative parameter.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

and associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. For every sequence
$(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets there is a sequence
$(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ with $a_n\in A_n$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$. Thus the
Axiom of Choice implies the pair-local countable choice principle
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Let $n,p\ge1$ be integers and let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ be a fixed matrix.
A **fixed-design first-moment linear regression model** is a parametric
statistical experiment on $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n))$ with parameter
set $\mathbb R^p$, laws $(P_\beta)_{\beta\in\mathbb R^p}$, and observed vector
$Y(y)=y$, such that every coordinate of $Y$ is integrable under $P_\beta$ and
$$
\mathbb E_\beta Y=X\beta\qquad(\beta\in\mathbb R^p).
$$
Here $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)$ is the Borel sigma-algebra, and expectation is
taken under the particular law $P_\beta$. The residual vector
$\epsilon_\beta:=Y-X\beta$ therefore has coordinatewise mean zero. The phrase
**fixed design** means that $X$ is held constant in this experiment; it carries
no probability law or assignment mechanism for $X$.

This definition states only the first-moment model. It imposes no covariance,
independence, or Gaussian assumption. Such assumptions must be stated where
used.

For integers $n,p\ge1$, a matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$, and a response
vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$, define the **least-squares solution set**
$$
\mathcal B_{\mathrm{LS}}(y):=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{b\in\mathbb R^p}\|y-Xb\|_2^2.
$$
This is a set-valued definition; it does not select one coefficient vector.
The next theorem proves that the set is nonempty and identifies the fitted
vector and residual as unique, including when $X$ is rank-deficient.

Let $n,p\ge1$, $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$, $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and
$C=\operatorname{col}(X)\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. For the least-squares solution
set $\mathcal B_{\mathrm{LS}}(y)$ of
[[def-least-squares-solution-set]], the following hold:

1. $\mathcal B_{\mathrm{LS}}(y)$ is nonempty, and $b$ is in it exactly when
   $X^T(Xb-y)=0$.
2. If $b_0\in\mathcal B_{\mathrm{LS}}(y)$, then
   $\mathcal B_{\mathrm{LS}}(y)=b_0+\ker X$.
3. Every least-squares solution has the same fitted vector $P_Cy$ and residual
   $y-P_Cy$.
4. The affine solution set has dimension $p-\operatorname{rank}(X)$.

The theorem makes no statistical moment or distributional assumption.

In a fixed-design first-moment regression model with $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$,
a contrast $c^T\beta$ is linearly estimable if and only if
$$
c\in\operatorname{row}(X)=\operatorname{im}(X^T),
$$
equivalently if and only if there exists $a\in\mathbb R^n$ with $X^Ta=c$.
Whenever this holds, $a^TY$ is unbiased for $c^T\beta$ for every $\beta$.
Here $\operatorname{row}(X)$ is defined as the image of the transpose map.

Let $(\mathcal F_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of sigma-algebras on a
probability space, and let $J_0,\dots,J_{m-1}\subseteq I$ be pairwise disjoint
index sets. For each $r<m$, define

$$\mathcal G_r:=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{i\in J_r}\mathcal F_i\right).$$

Then the sigma-algebras $\mathcal G_0,\dots,\mathcal G_{m-1}$ are independent.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

derivations.claim: Economy QR yields the unique least-squares coefficient, fitted projection, and residual decomposition.
An orthonormal basis adapted to the nested spaces turns the two residual sums into independent chi-square sums, proving the partial F law.
Orthogonal Gaussian coordinates prove the OLS normal law, coefficient-residual independence, chi-square residual law, exact contrast pivot, and contrast estimability.
At fixed variance the Gaussian likelihood is maximized by the least-squares minimizer.
The normal and F quantiles calibrate measurable tests at every null parameter, giving exact size.
Profiling the variance gives RSS/n almost surely; zero residual sum has no positive-variance maximizer, and residual mean square uses the distinct divisor n-p.

boundaries.reason: The model requires 1<=p<n and nonempty parameter space, so an empty observation or coefficient space is excluded.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement permits q=p, where the reduced design space is zero-dimensional, while nu remains positive.
The Statement permits p=1, q=1, or nu=1; step 2.1 uses positive chi-square degrees.
The Statement defines s=0 and RSS_F=0 branches; steps 2.1 and 4.1 show that event has probability zero and state the likelihood behavior.
The Statement restricts 0<alpha<1, and step 3.1 uses the unique t and F quantiles.
Step 1.2 and step 2.1 state where AC is used for normal laws and orthogonal coordinates; the finite algebra adds no arbitrary choice.

boundaries.reason: No biconditional is asserted; the estimability fact is used only in its row-space direction.
No biconditional is asserted by this item.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a deterministic full-column-rank matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ with $1\le p<n$, a parameter $\beta\in\mathbb R^p$, and $\sigma^2>0$. Observe $Y=X\beta+\epsilon$, where the coordinates of $\epsilon$ are independent with law $N(0,\sigma^2)$. This is the fixed-design Gaussian experiment on $\mathbb R^n$ indexed by $(\beta,\sigma^2)\in\mathbb R^p\times(0,\infty)$.

Let $\widehat\beta=(X^TX)^{-1}X^TY$, let $P_X$ be the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{col}X$, and define
$$RSS_F=\|(I_n-P_X)Y\|^2,\qquad \nu=n-p,\qquad s^2=RSS_F/\nu,\qquad s=\sqrt{s^2}.$$
For $c\in\mathbb R^p\setminus\{0\}$, set
$$T_c=\begin{cases}\dfrac{c^T\widehat\beta-c^T\beta}{s\sqrt{c^T(X^TX)^{-1}c}},&s>0,\\0,&s=0.\end{cases}$$
Then $\widehat\beta\sim N_p(\beta,\sigma^2(X^TX)^{-1})$, $\widehat\beta$ is independent of $RSS_F$, $RSS_F/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2_\nu$, $s>0$ almost surely, and $T_c\sim t_\nu$.

For a fixed reduced design $X_R\in\mathbb R^{n\times(p-q)}$ with $\operatorname{rank}X_R=p-q$, $\operatorname{col}X_R\subseteq\operatorname{col}X$, and $1\le q\le p$, put $W_R=\operatorname{col}X_R$ and
$$RSS_R=\|Y-P_{W_R}Y\|^2.$$
Under the null hypothesis $X\beta\in W_R$, the statistic
$$F=\begin{cases}\dfrac{(RSS_R-RSS_F)/q}{RSS_F/\nu},&RSS_F>0,\\0,&RSS_F=0\end{cases}$$
has law $F_{q,\nu}$. Both denominator degrees of freedom are positive; the empty reduced design space is allowed when $q=p$.

For a null value $\theta_0$, define $T_{c,\theta_0}$ by replacing $c^T\beta$ in the numerator of $T_c$ by $\theta_0$, with the same zero-denominator convention. For $0<\alpha<1$, the two-sided test of $H_0:c^T\beta=\theta_0$ that rejects when $|T_{c,\theta_0}|>t_{\nu,1-\alpha/2}$ has size exactly $\alpha$. The partial F test that rejects when $F>F^{-1}_{q,\nu}(1-\alpha)$ also has size exactly $\alpha$ under its stated null. The joint Gaussian maximum-likelihood estimate is $\widehat\beta$ together with $\widehat\sigma^2_{\rm ML}=RSS_F/n$ almost surely, distinct from $s^2=RSS_F/(n-p)$. If an observed vector has $RSS_F=0$, the likelihood has no maximizer over $\sigma^2>0$; this event has probability zero in the stated model.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment with $\Theta\ne\varnothing$, and let
$(S,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable space. A
family of measurable maps $q_\theta:\mathcal X\to S$, one for each
$\theta\in\Theta$, is a **pivot** if the pushforward law
$$\nu_\theta(B):=P_\theta(q_\theta^{-1}(B)),\qquad B\in\mathcal S$$
is the same probability measure $\nu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$.
Each section is a random element on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,P_\theta)$, so
its pushforward is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].
No measurability in $\theta$ is asserted or needed.

For $S=\mathbb R$, a pivot is a parameter-indexed family of measurable
real-valued quantities with a common sampling law. The maps $q_\theta$
may depend on the unknown parameter. A pivot need not be invertible in the
parameter, and its inversion need not be an interval.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment as in [[def-statistical-experiment]], and assume
$\Theta\ne\varnothing$. A **confidence-set procedure** is a map
$C:\mathcal X\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$, where
$\mathcal P(\Theta):=\{A:A\subseteq\Theta\}$, such that, for every
$\eta\in\Theta$, its
membership section
$$C_\eta:=\{x\in\mathcal X:\eta\in C(x)\}$$
belongs to $\mathcal A$. Its **coverage at $\theta$** is
$c_C(\theta):=P_\theta(C_\theta)$, and its **confidence level** is
$\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}c_C(\theta)$, the greatest lower bound of those
coverage values. For $0\le\alpha\le1$, it has coverage
at least $1-\alpha$ if $P_\theta(C_\theta)\ge1-\alpha$ for every
$\theta\in\Theta$.

Only membership sections need to be measurable; no sigma-algebra on the
parameter set is assumed. The parameter is fixed in the repeated-sampling
coverage probability.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be an
experiment with nonempty $\Theta$. Let $q_\theta:\mathcal X\to S$ be a
pivot with common law $\nu$, and let $B\in\mathcal S$. Define
$$C(x):=\{\theta\in\Theta:q_\theta(x)\in B\}$$
If $\nu(B)\ge1-\alpha$, then $C$ is a confidence set with coverage at
least $1-\alpha$. If $\nu(B)=1-\alpha$, its coverage is exactly
$1-\alpha$ for every parameter value. For an interval $B=[a,b]$ in
$\mathbb R$, exactness requires calibration of the actual probability
$\nu([a,b])$; quantile labels alone do not remove endpoint atoms.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every $k\ge1$, the CDF of $t_k$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$, is symmetric about zero, and has limits $0$ and $1$ at $-\infty$ and $+\infty$. For every $r,s\ge1$, the CDF of $F_{r,s}$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$, is zero on $(-\infty,0]$, and is strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$ with limit $1$ at $+\infty$. Consequently, for each $u\in(0,1)$ each law has exactly one $u$-quantile on its support.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a positive integer $k$, take the product probability law of an independent standard normal $G$ and an independent $Q_k\sim\chi_k^2$. The **Student t law with $k$ degrees of freedom**, denoted $t_k$, is the law of
$$T_k=\begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{G}{\sqrt{Q_k/k}},&Q_k>0,\\ 0,&Q_k\le0. \end{cases}$$
For positive integers $r,s$, take independent $Q_r\sim\chi_r^2$ and $Q_s\sim\chi_s^2$. The **Fisher F law with degrees $(r,s)$**, denoted $F_{r,s}$, is the law of
$$F_{r,s}=\begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{Q_r/r}{Q_s/s},&Q_s>0,\\ 0,&Q_s\le0. \end{cases}$$
The displayed piecewise maps are defined on all of $\mathbb R^2$ and are Borel measurable: each quotient is continuous on its Borel positive-denominator region, and the value on the complementary Borel nonpositive-denominator region is constant. The positive-degree chi-square lemma proves that the denominators are positive almost surely, so these versions agree almost surely with the usual quotients. Zero degrees are excluded from both definitions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For an integer $k\ge1$, let $G=(G_1,\ldots,G_k)$ have law $N_k(0,I_k)$, so its coordinates are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables. The **chi-square law with $k$ degrees of freedom**, denoted $\chi_k^2$, is the law of
$$
Q_k=\sum_{j=1}^k G_j^2=\|G\|^2.
$$
For $k=0$, define $\chi_0^2=\delta_0$, the point mass at zero. This zero-degree law records a rank-zero projection only; it is not used as a denominator in a Student or Fisher ratio. The multivariate-normal characteristic-function theorem makes the definition independent of the chosen realization of $G$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every integer $k\ge1$, the law $\chi_k^2$ has density
$$
f_k(x)=c_k x^{k/2-1}e^{-x/2}\mathbf 1_{\{x>0\}},\qquad c_k=\frac{\sigma_{k-1}(S^{k-1})}{2(2\pi)^{k/2}}>0,
$$
where $\sigma_{k-1}$ is the polar surface measure on the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^k$. Consequently, $Q_k>0$ almost surely, and its cumulative distribution function is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every $k\ge1$, the CDF of $t_k$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$, is symmetric about zero, and has limits $0$ and $1$ at $-\infty$ and $+\infty$. For every $r,s\ge1$, the CDF of $F_{r,s}$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$, is zero on $(-\infty,0]$, and is strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$ with limit $1$ at $+\infty$. Consequently, for each $u\in(0,1)$ each law has exactly one $u$-quantile on its support.

Use the fixed full-column-rank Gaussian regression model and notation of [[thm-exact-gaussian-linear-regression-inference]], with $\nu=n-p$. Let $0<\alpha<1$, let $t^*=t_{\nu,1-\alpha/2}$ be the unique $(1-\alpha/2)$ quantile of $t_\nu$, and put $v_c=c^T(X^TX)^{-1}c$ for $c\ne0$. Then
$$C_c(Y)=\left[c^T\widehat\beta-t^*s\sqrt{v_c},\ c^T\widehat\beta+t^*s\sqrt{v_c}\right]$$
has exact coverage $1-\alpha$ for $c^T\beta$.

For any $x_0\in\mathbb R^p$, put $h_0=x_0^T(X^TX)^{-1}x_0$. The mean-response interval
$$C_{\rm mean}(Y;x_0)=\left[x_0^T\widehat\beta-t^*s\sqrt{h_0},\ x_0^T\widehat\beta+t^*s\sqrt{h_0}\right]$$
has exact coverage $1-\alpha$ for $x_0^T\beta$ when $x_0\ne0$. If $x_0=0$, it is the singleton $\{0\}$ and has coverage $1$.

If $Y_0^*=x_0^T\beta+\epsilon_0^*$ is one future response with $\epsilon_0^*\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ independent of the training data, then
$$C_{\rm pred}(Y;x_0)=\left[x_0^T\widehat\beta-t^*s\sqrt{1+h_0},\ x_0^T\widehat\beta+t^*s\sqrt{1+h_0}\right]$$
satisfies $\mathbb P_{\beta,\sigma^2}\{Y_0^*\in C_{\rm pred}(Y;x_0)\}=1-\alpha$. The added $1$ is the variance contribution of the future response's own error.
